title: Checkpoint: Banks and Borrowing
objective: After this level you can explain how banks, interest and credit work together, and the risks of debt.
summary: Credit comes from Latin credere, to trust. A loan is born as a new deposit and destroyed when repaid. Interest, collateral, scores and bank runs all turn on trust.

cards.headline: Every loan in this chapter ran on one word: believe.
cards.body: "Credit" comes from the Latin credere, to trust or believe. Time to see how that trust ties banks, interest and debt together.

cards.headline: Credit means trust
cards.body: The Latin creditum meant a loan, a thing entrusted to another, from credere: to trust, entrust, believe. This whole chapter is that word at work. A borrower is trusted to repay, and interest is the price paid for the loan. A credit score is a lender's prediction of how likely you are to pay a loan back on time.

events.label: The bank credits a new deposit: new money (Level 22)
On a secured loan, the lender can take the collateral (Level 28)
Repaying the loan destroys the money it created (Level 22)

cards.headline: When belief cracks
cards.body: Trust runs the other way too. A bank run is when many depositors try to withdraw at once, and it can put a bank out of business. Deposit insurance exists to keep public confidence steady. From Level 6's banknotes to Level 29's queues, money and credit work because people believe they will.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: Why credit means trust, and how a bank creates new money every time it makes a loan.
How interest works as rent for money, and why compounding makes both savings and debts snowball.
What makes a loan cost more or less: collateral, your credit record and how long you borrow.
Why no bank can pay all its depositors at once, and how a bank run feeds on its own fear.

questions.prompt: The word credit comes from Latin credere. What did credere mean?

options.label: To count or measure
options.rationale: Credere is about trust, not counting.

options.label: To trust or believe
To lend at interest
options.rationale: The root meaning is trust; lending grew out of it.

options.label: To buy or sell
options.rationale: Credere meant to trust, entrust or believe.

questions.explanation: Credere meant 'to trust, entrust, believe', and creditum was a loan, a thing entrusted to another.

questions.prompt: You make the final payment on a bank loan. What happens to the money that loan created?

options.label: It moves into the central bank's reserves
options.rationale: Repayment destroys it rather than moving it.

options.label: It becomes the bank's profit
options.rationale: The bank's profit comes from interest; the loan money itself is destroyed.

options.label: It is destroyed
It is sent back to the original saver
options.rationale: No saver's money was lent: the loan created the deposit.

questions.explanation: Lending creates a deposit; repaying the loan destroys it.

questions.prompt: An unpaid card balance at about 22% a year grows faster each year. Which idea explains that?

options.label: Compound interest: interest charged on earlier interest
Simple interest charged only on the first purchase
options.rationale: Simple interest would grow by the same amount each year.

options.label: Deposit insurance limits
options.rationale: Insurance protects deposits; it has nothing to do with card debt.

options.label: The Minimum Payment Warning adding fees
options.rationale: The warning is a disclosure, not a charge.

questions.explanation: Unpaid interest joins the balance and is charged interest too, so the debt snowballs.

questions.prompt: Why does a car loan usually carry a lower rate than an unsecured personal loan?

options.label: Cars never lose value
options.rationale: The point is that the lender can take the car.

options.label: Personal loans are banned from being cheap
options.rationale: No such rule: the difference is risk.

options.label: Car buyers always have higher credit scores
options.rationale: Scores vary. Collateral is what lowers the lender's risk.

options.label: The car is collateral, so the lender takes less risk

questions.explanation: Secured loans are less risky for lenders, so they usually carry lower interest rates.

questions.prompt: What do a credit score and a bank run have in common, in this chapter?

options.label: Both are set by the central bank
options.rationale: Neither is set by a central bank.

options.label: Both are about trust that money will be repaid
Both only happen with credit cards
options.rationale: Runs hit banks; scores cover all kinds of borrowing.

options.label: Both were invented in 1933
options.rationale: 1933 is when the FDIC was created.

questions.explanation: A score measures how far a lender can trust a borrower; a run is what happens when depositors stop trusting a bank. Credit means trust.
